study.title: Exodus 26 The structure, the roofs and limits of the tabernacle
study.overview: Exodus 26 details the construction of the tabernacle accurately: the inner curtains, the outer roofs, the boards and bars that support the structure, the veil that separates the holy place from the most holy and the curtain of the entrance. The chapter shows that God's abode among the people is not improvised, but organized according to a model received by Moses on the mountain. The repetition of measurements, fittings, brackets and bases highlights order, stability and holy separation. At the same time, the text preserves an important tension: God dwells among the people, but their holiness also establishes restricted and mediated access.

outline.title: Internal curtains and union of the tabernacle
outline.explanation: The ten curtains of fine linen with blue, purple, crimson and cherubim form the main cover. Five are joined to five, with loops and gold brackets, so that the set becomes one piece. The notes highlight that the final piece covered the ceiling and walls of the tabernacle, forming the noblest part of the structure.

outline.title: External hair covers and skins
outline.explanation: On the inner cover come the curtains of goat hair, larger, connected with bronze brackets, and then the sheepskin dyed red and another top cover. The effect is double: protection against climate and preservation of internal beauty. The comments note that external coverage was broader to engage the internal one and that the simplest connections also served to unite firmly.

outline.title: Boards, bases and bars that support housing
outline.explanation: The acacia wood boards, supported on silver bases, form the south, north and western sides, including the corner pieces. The acacia wood bars, coated with gold, reinforce the unit of the structure. The text insists that everything be done according to the model shown on the mount, which underlines detailed obedience and not human invention.

outline.title: Veal, interior layout and curtain of the entrance
outline.explanation: The veil of entry into the most holy place separates the holy one from the most holy and protects the ark of the testimony. Then the table and the chandelier are placed according to the orientation given, and the entrance receives a similar curtain, supported by five columns with bronze bases. The chapter ends by showing that the presence of God is real, but surrounded by holiness, distinction and mediation.

study.context: The chapter describes the tabernacle of Israel in the wilderness as a movable and carefully ordained dwelling. The notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry treat the structure as suitable for the pilgrim condition of the people, something that could be transported and assembled as the journey. The focus of the text is not in luxury in itself, but in representing God's presence among his people in a holy, controlled and reverent way. There is no material in the material provided a specific date or an additional archaeological context to be stated safely.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that God decides how to be worshipped and how to dwell in the midst of his people. The precision of the project shows that divine holiness cannot be treated improvised. The beautiful curtains, simple roofs, strong boards and different metal bases suggest a harmony between glory and protection, beauty and endurance, proximity and separation. The veil is especially important: he reveals that access to the most intimate presence of God in that covenant was limited and mediated. At the same time, the tabernacle itself is a sign of grace: God accepts to live among a people in motion, accommodating their presence to their condition. The readings of Henry and Clarke also see a typological value, that is, the tabernacle points to later realities; this is a valid devotional interpretation, but should not be treated as the only obligatory conclusion of the text.

scholarViews.insight: The two curtain covers, united together, formed a single unit that served at the same time walls and ceiling of the tabernacle.
God adjusts the signs of his presence to the needs of his people in the wilderness, giving them a mobile dwelling according to their condition.
The inner veil represented a real separation between the holy and the most holy place, and the name of the veil suggests this idea of division.

questions: What does the thorough care of God in ordering the tabernacle teaches about reverence in worship?
How does the veil, which separates the saint from the most holy, helps to understand the holiness of God and the limits of human access?
How can the combination of beauty, endurance and mobility in the tabernacle guide the life of faith in times of walking and instability?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to value the planned, reverent and obedient worship. In practice, this means not treating the presence of God with improvisation or superficiality, but seeking order, purity, and faithfulness to what he reveals. It also teaches how to balance two attitudes: to approach God with confidence and at the same time with holy fear. In concrete terms, it is worth reviewing the devotional life itself, the worship and posture in Christian service to express beauty, integrity and submission to the will of God.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the structural and theological function of the tabernacle, but do not authorize additional details about manufacturing, accurate chronology, materials in addition to the aforementioned or extensive historical interpretations. The typological readings of some commentators should be understood as interpretations, not as the unique and unequivocal meaning of the text.
